<reason>Both sides ran a sophisticated, well-matched case, but A built the more durable path to victory. A's core move—that the "evidence asymmetry" B relies on is partly self-inflicted (agencies have decades of pricing data because they only looked for pricing harm) and that "every market is messy at the edges" (grocery markets have delivery apps, warehouse clubs, etc., just as labor markets have telehealth and cross-training)—directly undercut B's central structural claim without ever being squarely rebutted. A also used the Penguin Random House precedent effectively on both sides of the exchange: B tried to spin it as proof discretion already works, but A correctly noted this cuts against B's "structurally unmeasurable" claim by showing the tools were used successfully. A's closing crystallized the debate well: once B conceded in A1 that "proven" means the ordinary preponderance standard, the remaining objection collapsed into "don't routinely check," which A turned into a memorable and damaging line ("a coin never tossed... has a thumb on it"). B's strongest surviving point—the distinction between firm-specific efficiency verification (easy discovery) and market-power estimation (irreducibly noisy)—was a genuinely sharp and under-addressed argument, especially since A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped right as it approached this exact issue, and A's closing did not return to it. This is a real, uncompensated gap in A's case. However, A's clipping (twice) is an execution cost, not a substantive concession, and A had already landed the "messy markets are universal" and "self-inflicted asymmetry" points earlier that undermine the foundation of B's distinction even if not explicitly reapplied to it. On balance, A's normative framing (the status quo asymmetry is a policy choice, not a neutral fact) proved more resilient across the exchange, while B's case increasingly relied on implementation-level objections that never fully answered why routinely asking the question is worse than never asking it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 point that "every market is messy at the edges" (grocery markets include delivery apps, warehouse clubs, Amazon) directly undercut B's foundational claim that price-market definition is clean while labor-market definition is uniquely noisy—a point B never squarely re-defended in Rebuttal 2 or Closing, leaving it live for A through the end.</best_rebuttal>
